limits.description: Article 75 of the Convention Implementing the Schengen Agreement (CISA) lets travelers carry 'the narcotic drugs and psychotropic substances that are necessary for their medical treatment' if, at any check, they can produce a certificate issued or authenticated by a competent authority of their state of residence. Article 75 itself leaves the certificate's exact form and the details on permitted quantity and journey duration to the Schengen Executive Committee; in practice the resulting 'Schengen certificate' is understood to cover only the quantity needed for a journey of up to 30 days.
limits.quantity: up to a 30-day supply, evidenced by the Schengen certificate

notes: This is a Schengen-wide legal basis (confirmed directly from Article 75's text), but the certificate itself is issued nationally — by a doctor, pharmacist, or health authority depending on the member state — before you travel; there is no single EU-wide online portal. Article 75 covers 'narcotic drugs and psychotropic substances' as legal classes rather than naming individual medicines, but these classes are the internationally scheduled categories (1961 and 1971 UN conventions) that cover common stimulants (Adderall/amphetamine, Vyvanse/lisdexamfetamine, Ritalin/methylphenidate), benzodiazepines (Xanax/alprazolam, Valium/diazepam, Klonopin/clonazepam), and opioid painkillers (codeine, oxycodone, tramadol). Some Schengen states still restrict or ban specific substances outright under their own national law regardless of the certificate — for example, the UK's own guidance (a non-Schengen state, cited here only as an illustration of the pattern) notes a Schengen certificate cannot be used to bring a Schedule 1 drug into Great Britain. Confirm with the specific member state's narcotics authority before traveling with an unusual medication.

legal_source.name: Convention Implementing the Schengen Agreement, Art. 75

limits.description: Kenya Revenue Authority's traveler FAQ lists 'Narcotic drugs' among goods prohibited for import outright (citing the 2nd and 3rd Schedule of the East African Community Customs Management Act), while listing 'Medicaments' generally among restricted goods that may be imported once 'authorization by relevant Government Institutions' is obtained. The FAQ does not say which of these two rules governs a specific controlled prescription medicine (e.g. a stimulant, benzodiazepine, or opioid painkiller), does not name the authorizing institution for medicaments, and states no personal-use quantity or day-supply exception.

notes: This is a genuine, unresolved gap in KRA's public guidance, not a confirmed 'allowed' or 'banned' answer. Kenya's controlling law for scheduled drugs is the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (Control) Act, 1994, and the Pharmacy and Poisons Board is Kenya's medicines regulator, but no traveler-facing page from either body could be reached in this pass (pharmacyboardkenya.org returned an expired-certificate error; NACADA's site had no relevant guidance) to confirm whether a foreign prescription is sufficient or a specific permit is required. Anyone carrying an ADHD stimulant, benzodiazepine, or opioid painkiller should contact a Kenyan diplomatic mission or the Pharmacy and Poisons Board before travel rather than assume the ordinary prescription-medication allowance covers it.

The guide does not specify which rule governs a specific controlled prescription medicine — e.g. an ADHD stimulant, a benzodiazepine, or an opioid painkiller — so it cannot be confirmed from this source alone whether such medication is treated as an allowed personal medicine or a prohibited habit-forming drug.

notes: South Africa separately schedules narcotics/psychotropics under the Medicines and Related Substances Act (Schedules 5 and 6) and the Drugs and Drug Trafficking Act, administered by SAHPRA and SAPS respectively, but no SAHPRA or SAPS page addressing a traveler's personal-use import of scheduled substances could be reached in this pass — SAHPRA's public import-permit pages (importation-of-medical-products-border-control) describe commercial/institutional importation processes, not personal baggage. Given SARS's own guide leaves the 'habit-forming drug' vs 'personal medicine' classification unresolved for controlled prescription drugs, travelers carrying stimulants, benzodiazepines, or opioid painkillers should carry the original prescription plus a doctor's letter and confirm status with SAHPRA or a South African diplomatic mission before travel.

Under Mexico's Ley General de Salud, 'sustancias psicotrópicas' is the class that covers common controlled stimulants (e.g. amphetamine/Adderall, methylphenidate/Ritalin, lisdexamfetamine/Vyvanse) and benzodiazepines (e.g. alprazolam/Xanax, diazepam/Valium, clonazepam/Klonopin), so a doctor's prescription for these should be sufficient for personal-use quantities at the border.

notes: ANAM's traveler-facing text names only 'sustancias psicotrópicas' (psychotropic substances) — it does not mention 'estupefacientes' (narcotic drugs), the separate Mexican legal category that covers opioid painkillers such as codeine, oxycodone, and tramadol. Whether the same simple prescription-only rule extends to opioid painkillers, or whether they instead require the more formal COFEPRIS sanitary import permit used for controlled narcotics (Permiso Sanitario COFEPRIS-03-023, aimed primarily at commercial/institutional importers), is not addressed by ANAM's page, so opioid painkillers are deliberately left out of this entry's name list. No numeric day-supply or unit-quantity cap is published for psychotropics either. Travelers carrying opioid painkillers should confirm with COFEPRIS (tel. 800 033 5050) or a Mexican consulate before travel.

The glucose-meter allowance strongly implies diabetes supplies are contemplated by this rule, but a sharps/needle-specific declaration requirement could not be confirmed. Carry the medication in original packaging with your prescription or a doctor's letter, and declare injector pens/needles if asked.

Treat the detention reports as an important caution rather than a verified fact, and do not assume a specific controlled medication is covered by the general 'medications for personal use' allowance. limits.description: All of the following are listed by name on the UAE's official controlled/semi-controlled medicines schedule and are allowed for personal use ONLY with supporting documents, up to a maximum 3-month supply: amphetamine (Adderall), lisdexamfetamine (Vyvanse), methylphenidate (Ritalin) — Psychotropic Schedule II; alprazolam (Xanax), diazepam (Valium), clonazepam (Klonopin) — Psychotropic Schedule IV / 'CD'; codeine, oxycodone — Narcotic Schedule I/II; tramadol — 'CD'. None of these is flatly prohibited. Travelers must carry BOTH a dated, stamped prescription (issued within 3 months) AND an attested medical report (issued within 1 year) naming the medicine, dose, and treatment duration.
limits.quantity: up to a 3-month supply (or the length of stay, whichever is less)

notes: The Emirates Drug Establishment (EDE) — which took over the Ministry of Health and Prevention's (MOHAP) controlled-medicines functions on 29 Dec 2025 under Federal Decree-Law No. 38 of 2024 — offers an optional electronic pre-approval permit before travel; it is NOT strictly mandatory, and travelers may instead simply declare the medicine with prescription + medical report at the port of entry. In practice, undeclared or undocumented controlled medication is what has led to detentions at UAE airports historically, even for drugs that are technically allowed with paperwork — this row corrects the common assumption (from older secondary press reporting) that these drugs are outright banned; per EDE's own current list they are not, but the documentation bar (prescription AND medical report, not just prescription alone) is stricter than most countries. This list is dated 15/09/2022 by EDE/MOHAP but remains the current published schedule as of Sept 2026; it explicitly states non-inclusion of a substance doesn't mean it's uncontrolled, so travelers with any other controlled medication should verify against EDE directly. MOHAP's own domain (mohap.gov.ae) was unreachable during this research (connection resets), so EDE.gov.ae — confirmed as the current regulator via the Federal Decree-Law — was used instead.

legal_source.name: Emirates Drug Establishment (EDE) — Issue of Permit to Import Medicines for Personal Use / Controlled and Semi-Controlled Medicines List

limits.description: The quantity of medicines (including biologics) carried in accompanied baggage must be compatible with personal use/consumption and with the circumstances and length of the trip — there is no fixed numeric day-supply cap. A medical prescription signed by a qualified professional may be requested by the health authority at the port of entry if the quantity does not look consistent with your stay or suggests commercial resale.

notes: This is Brazil's general 'accompanied baggage' rule and applies to ordinary prescription and OTC medicines, biologics, and medical products alike. Narcotic and psychotropic ('controlled') medicines are governed by a separate, much stricter ANVISA import regime — see the dedicated 'controlled medication' entry for this destination.

legal_source.name: ANVISA (Agência Nacional de Vigilância Sanitária) — Regras de bagagem (Portos, aeroportos e fronteiras)

limits.description: Whether a controlled medicine can be imported depends on which of ANVISA's schedules (Lists A1, A2, A3, B1, B2, C1–C5, set by Portaria SVS/MS n° 344/1998) its active substance is on. Medicines on List C1 may be brought in with only a valid medical prescription shown to the sanitary authority at the port of entry — no advance ANVISA authorization is needed, provided no similar product is registered/sold in Brazil (commercial sale of the imported product is prohibited; personal use only). Medicines on Lists A1, A2, A3, B1, B2, C2 and C5 cannot be imported by a traveler at all without ANVISA's advance, case-by-case 'exceptional use' authorization: the patient/legal guardian must petition before travel through ANVISA's SEI electronic system with a signed prescription (patient name, commercial drug name, dosage, quantity, treatment duration, doctor's signature/CRM), a medical report (diagnosis/CID, case history, justification vs. Brazilian-registered alternatives), and a signed liability statement. Approval is not guaranteed and, once granted, must be presented at the ANVISA airport post to release the medicine.

notes: Substances on List C3 (teratogenic/immunosuppressant, e.g. thalidomide, lenalidomide, pomalidomide) are excluded even from the exceptional-use pathway. Substances on Lists E and F are proscribed outright — import, export, trade and use are illegal for any purpose other than authorized research. This pass verified the mechanism directly from ANVISA's official 'Importação de produtos controlados' page, but did not cross-check the live substance-by-substance annex (Portaria 344/1998, Anexo I, which is amended periodically by separate RDCs) to confirm exactly which list captures each named drug — e.g. whether Adderall/amphetamine, Xanax/alprazolam, Valium/diazepam, Klonopin/clonazepam, codeine, oxycodone or tramadol individually sit on C1 versus one of the prohibited-without-authorization lists. Confirm your specific medicine's list before travel via ANVISA's published substance list or its helpline (0800 642 9782).

legal_source.name: ANVISA — Importação de produtos controlados (Medicamentos)

limits.description: Insulin and GLP-1 injectable medicines (semaglutide/Ozempic/Wegovy, tirzepatide/Mounjaro/Zepbound) fall under 'medicamentos, incluindo os biológicos' in ANVISA's baggage rules: the personal-use quantity must be compatible with your treatment and length of stay in Brazil, with no fixed numeric day-supply cap published. A medical prescription may be requested if the quantity looks excessive for the trip. Needles, syringes and pen injectors are 'produtos médicos' (medical products) under the same personal-use rule.

notes: None of these substances are narcotics or psychotropics under Portaria 344/1998, so the stricter ANVISA controlled-substances import regime (see the 'controlled medication' entry for Brazil) does not apply to them. ANVISA's baggage-rules page does not name insulin, semaglutide, tirzepatide, or needles specifically — it addresses them only through the general 'biológicos'/'produtos médicos' categories — so no drug-specific guidance (e.g. sharps handling, a syringe-count cap) was found on a primary source in this pass.

limits.description: Up to 3 months' supply for your own or an immediate family member's use, provided the medicine is lawfully prescribed to you in your country of residence, does not contain a controlled substance (see the 'controlled medication' entry) or a prohibited substance, and is not in chewing-gum form. Tramadol was checked against the same list and was NOT found on it, so ordinary medicine (not the controlled-substances process) rules appear to apply to it — but confirm against the live Appendix A before travel, since HSA updates it periodically. limits.description: Individuals may cross the U.S. border with a Schedule II-V controlled substance for personal medical use if (1) it is in the original container it was dispensed in, and (2) the traveler declares it to a CBP officer, stating either the trade/chemical name and schedule, or the prescribing practitioner/pharmacy and prescription number. limits.description: As FDA-approved prescription drugs, GLP-1 medications (semaglutide/tirzepatide) and insulin follow the FDA's personal importation framework: foreign visitors may bring in roughly a 90-day supply, with the prescription or a doctor's letter. limits.description: Up to 3 months' supply of medicine containing a controlled drug can be carried in hand luggage without a Home Office licence. limits.description: Liquid medication over 100ml (which covers most injectable pens/vials) is allowed through UK airport security in hand luggage, but you must carry proof it's prescribed to you -- a prescription copy or a letter from your doctor. limits.description: Under CBSA's Section 56 Class Exemption, travelers may personally carry (in person only -- not by mail or courier) a prescribed narcotic or Food and Drug Regulations Part G controlled drug up to the lesser of a single course of treatment or a 30-day supply, and a prescribed benzodiazepine/targeted substance up to the lesser of a single course of treatment or a 90-day supply. Disposable vapes were reportedly banned nationwide in April 2025 — a separate, more recent development not covered by the Q&A document cited here.

legal_source.name: Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare (MHLW) — Q&A on Pharmaceutical Import Procedures (医薬品等輸入手続質疑応答集)

limits.description: Since around August 2020, Saudi Customs has banned individuals from importing e-cigarettes, shisha and their accessories through shipping companies and personal website purchases — goods imported this way are confiscated, a fine is imposed, and a seizure record is registered. Companies licensed by the Saudi Food and Drug Authority (SFDA) may still import these products in commercial quantities.

notes: This measure is specifically about shipping/mail-order/online-purchase import channels for individuals — it does not clearly say whether it also restricts what a traveler personally carries in accompanied luggage, and that distinction wasn't confirmed either way in this pass. Don't assume it's safe to bring a personal vape in checked or carry-on baggage just because this rule targets shipping specifically — but also don't assume accompanied baggage is covered by the same ban. Corroborated identically across 5 independent outlets (Saudi Gazette, Zawya, Al Bawaba, Riyadh Xpress, Vaping Post); every direct fetch of the Saudi Gazette article itself returned HTTP 402 (paywalled), so this is strong multi-source corroboration rather than a directly read primary article. Separately, Arab News (directly fetched and quoted) traces the same underlying policy back further: the Ministry of Commerce and Investment banned e-cigarette/vaping sales in September 2015, and "considers anyone bringing them in from abroad to be smuggling" — broader phrasing than 'shipping only' — so the individual-import restriction isn't a one-off report, it's a long-standing, consistently-described policy, even though the accompanied-baggage question specifically remains unresolved. Domestic sale/possession has separately been legal since Royal Decree 38621 (2019) — don't confuse 'legal to own in Saudi Arabia' with 'legal to personally import.'

legal_source.name: Saudi Gazette — 'Customs ban individuals from importing electronic cigarettes' (c. August 2020)

limits.description: Vaping products aren't mentioned anywhere on NZ Customs' own duty-free FAQ page, and aren't covered by the tobacco-specific concession (limited to 50 cigarettes, or 50g of cigars/tobacco/a mixture) — so they fall under the general goods concession instead: "You'll have to pay GST and duty if you bought more than NZ$700 in total" of duty-free items and related purchases.

notes: This corrects a previously-uncorroborated claim of a '3 month supply' vape-specific allowance, which doesn't appear anywhere on NZ Customs' actual site — the real rule is simpler: no vape-specific concession exists, so the general $700 threshold governs instead. Vaping products are regulated inside New Zealand (a disposable-vape sales ban, retailer age-verification rules) rather than at the border specifically.

legal_source.name: New Zealand Customs Service — Duty-Free Shopping FAQs

limits.description: "Saudi law prohibits importation of the following products: weapons, alcohol, narcotics, pork and pork products..." — pork and pork products are absolutely prohibited, no exceptions. Separately, "the importation of the following products requires special approval by Saudi authorities: ... live animals ..." — live animals need advance authorization before import.

notes: Directly quoted from a U.S. government trade guide, not a Saudi government page itself (ZATCA's and SFDA's own prohibited-goods pages remain unreachable — 404s and unreadable scanned PDFs, a persistent block for this project on Saudi domains). This source is specific about pork and live animals but doesn't state a general rule for other meat or dairy products — don't assume non-pork meat or dairy is unrestricted just because it isn't named here; it simply wasn't confirmed either way in this pass.

legal_source.name: U.S. International Trade Administration — Saudi Arabia: Prohibited and Restricted Imports

limits.description: "The importation of the following products requires special approval by Saudi authorities: agricultural seeds ..." — quoted directly. Seeds need advance authorization from Saudi authorities before import.

notes: This source confirms a special-approval requirement for agricultural seeds specifically — it doesn't separately address general fresh fruit and vegetables, so treat this row as covering seeds only, not a blanket fresh-produce rule, until a broader source is found.

legal_source.name: U.S. International Trade Administration — Saudi Arabia: Prohibited and Restricted Imports

limits.description: Ministry of Agriculture and Land Reclamation Decree 1647 (1997) requires importers to apply to the General Organization for Veterinary Services (GOVS) for a permit before bringing in meat/animal products, with the epidemiological status of the country of origin taken into account; a granted permit is valid for 1 month and is renewable.

notes: The decree's own text and the USDA report describing it are both unreadable in this environment (scanned/binary PDFs) — this is drawn from the report's search-indexed summary rather than a directly read document, similar in tier to how this project has cited a USDA GAIN report for a different country's regulation elsewhere. The permit mechanism reads as built for commercial importers, similar to Kenya's meat-import regulation already in this dataset — no traveler/personal-quantity carve-out was found, so don't assume it applies the same way to a tourist's suitcase as to a commercial shipment. Egypt's National Food Safety Authority took over food-safety regulation generally in 2020 but still relies on GOVS for this specific import-permit mechanism.

legal_source.name: USDA FAS GAIN Report — FAIRS Country Report Annual, Cairo Egypt (EG2025-0025), re: Ministry of Agriculture and Land Reclamation Decree 1647 (1997)

limits.description: "The medicines are allowed with a maximum of 6 bottles or three months' supply." Travelers must show proof the medicines are for personal use — a prescription, medical certificate or pharmacy label on the packaging — and may also be asked for a receipt or other proof of lawful purchase. Keep medicines in their original packaging.

notes: This is for ordinary, non-narcotic medication — medicines containing controlled substances follow a separate advance-permit process (see the dedicated controlled-medication entry for Korea).

legal_source.name: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Korea, Embassy Notice — Bringing Medicines into Korea by Travel

limits.description: "Any person who will enter into Korea with medicines containing controlled substances should get a permit from the Ministry [of Food and Drug Safety, MFDS], regardless of their nationality" — quoted directly. In force since October 23, 2009; online applications available since December 27, 2024. Apply in advance through MFDS's Narcotics Policy Division (+82-43-719-1564, narcotics@korea.kr).

notes: Amphetamine-based stimulants (Adderall, Vyvanse, Dexedrine) are consistently reported elsewhere as treated as narcotics that cannot be brought in for personal use even with a valid prescription or MFDS permit — this specific amphetamine-vs-methylphenidate distinction is corroborated across multiple independent travel/relocation sites but wasn't read verbatim in a primary MFDS document in this pass. Methylphenidate (Ritalin/Concerta) is legal but still requires the same MFDS narcotics-import permit as any other controlled medication. Travelers carrying amphetamine-based medication have reportedly faced detention or questioning, since it can register similarly to methamphetamine on a drug test.

legal_source.name: Ministry of Food and Drug Safety (Korea) — permit requirement for entering Korea with medicines containing controlled substances

limits.description: Narcotic/addictive medication (thuốc gây nghiện): up to a 7-day supply per the accompanying prescription's dosage, carried without needing a separate export/import permit. Psychotropic drugs and precursor-containing medication (thuốc hướng thần, tiền chất): up to a 10-day supply. Combination medications containing narcotic, psychotropic, precursor, toxic or banned substances together: up to a 30-day supply. Exceeding these thresholds requires an export/import permit. A copy of the prescription and medical records, certified by a healthcare organization or bearing a signature/stamp, must accompany the medication.

notes: These figures are extremely well-established and consistently repeated across many independent Vietnamese sources, including a Vietnam Customs regional office (kv17.customs.gov.vn) page titled exactly on this topic — but that page (like most Vietnamese customs.gov.vn pages throughout this project's research) is JS-rendered and its body text couldn't be directly extracted, so the specific figures here are search-engine-corroborated rather than read verbatim from a primary source. The exact governing circular/decree number is also genuinely unresolved: one commonly-repeated attribution to Circular 19/2014/TT-BYT Art. 17 turned out to be a misattribution (that article is about export/import licensing procedures, not traveler carry limits) when checked directly, and neither of that circular's two known successors (20/2017/TT-BYT, 18/2026/TT-BYT) contain the traveler provision either — treat the day-supply figures as reliable, the specific legal citation as unconfirmed.

legal_source.name: Chi cục Hải quan khu vực XVII (Vietnam Customs, Region XVII) — Quy định về mang thuốc cá nhân khi xuất cảnh (Regulations on carrying personal medication when departing)

limits.description: "进出境人员随身携带的个人自用的少量药品，应当以自用、合理数量为限，并接受海关监管" ("Small quantities of medication for personal use carried by inbound/outbound persons shall be limited to self-use, reasonable quantities, and subject to customs supervision") — Art. 39, Measures for the Administration of Drug Import. There's no fixed numeric cap in the regulation itself; it's a "self-use, reasonable quantity" standard applied at customs' discretion. Multiple municipal-government FAQ pages commonly describe this as interpreted around a 3-month supply in practice, with a prescription, doctor's certificate, or purchase receipts as proof of legitimate personal use.

notes: Narcotic drugs and psychotropic substances follow a separate, stricter framework — see the dedicated controlled-medication entry for China.

legal_source.name: 药品进口管理办法 (Measures for the Administration of Drug Import), Art. 39 — jointly issued by NMPA (formerly SFDA) and the General Administration of Customs

limits.description: "因治疗疾病需要，个人凭医疗机构出具的医疗诊断书、本人身份证明，可以携带单张处方最大用量以内的麻醉药品和第一类精神药品" ("For treatment of illness, an individual, upon presenting a medical diagnosis certificate issued by a medical institution and personal ID, may carry narcotic drugs and Category I psychotropic substances not exceeding the maximum quantity of a single prescription") — Art. 44, Regulations on the Administration of Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (State Council Order No. 442). Without this documentation, expect much stricter scrutiny. Healthcare workers carrying such drugs for medical duty need a certificate from a provincial drug-supervision department instead.

notes: Which specific common Western medications (e.g. Adderall/amphetamine-class ADHD stimulants) count as "Category I psychotropic substances" under China's own drug schedule was not independently confirmed against a named-substance list in this pass — China's well-documented strict stance on ADHD stimulants makes it very likely they fall under this framework and require the same documentation, but don't assume a specific drug is covered or excluded without checking. Opium, morphine, heroin, cannabis and other addictive narcotics are separately absolutely prohibited for import/export under a different customs order, corroborated by search but not independently re-verified this pass.

legal_source.name: 麻醉药品和精神药品管理条例 (Regulations on the Administration of Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances), State Council Order No. 442, Art. 44

limits.description: "A passenger aged 18 or above is allowed to bring into Hong Kong, for his own use, 1 litre of alcoholic liquor with an alcoholic strength above 30% by volume" duty-free (measured at 20℃). Hong Kong ID card holders must have spent 24 hours or more outside Hong Kong to claim it.

notes: The 1-litre concession only matters for spirits: Hong Kong's duty schedule charges 0% on wine and on liquor other than wine of 30% ABV or less, so beer and wine aren't dutiable. Passengers who fail to declare, or make a false or incomplete declaration of, dutiable goods above the concession are liable to prosecution under the Dutiable Commodities Ordinance.

legal_source.name: Hong Kong Customs and Excise Department — Duty-free Concessions

limits.description: "A passenger aged 18 or above is allowed to bring into Hong Kong, for his own use, the following quantity of tobacco products exempted from duty: 19 cigarettes; or 1 cigar or 25 grams of cigars; or 25 grams of other manufactured tobacco."
limits.quantity: 19 cigarettes, or 1 cigar / 25 g of cigars, or 25 g other manufactured tobacco

notes: One of the smallest tobacco allowances in the world — a single pack of 20 exceeds it. Passengers who fail to declare excess dutiable goods are liable to prosecution. E-cigarettes and heated tobacco are a separate, stricter matter: see the e-cigarettes entry for Hong Kong.

legal_source.name: Hong Kong Customs and Excise Department — Duty-free Concessions

limits.description: Anyone arriving at a specified control point with currency and bearer negotiable instruments totalling "more than HKD120,000" must "make a declaration to a Customs officer, using the Red Channel." The threshold applies in any currency (declare in the original currency, e.g. USD 20,000); an adult accompanying a child under 16 declares on the child's behalf.

notes: Maximum penalty for failing to declare or disclose is a fine of HK$500,000 and two years' imprisonment. A first-time breach can be settled by paying HK$2,000 if the traveller has no prior money-laundering or terrorist-financing conviction and the money isn't suspected crime proceeds. Hong Kong has no currency import cap, only this declaration duty.

legal_source.name: Hong Kong Customs and Excise Department — Currency and Bearer Negotiable Instruments

limits.description: "No person may import an alternative smoking product by way of parcels, cargoes, and bringing in by incoming travellers." The ban covers e-cigarettes, heated tobacco (heat sticks), herbal cigarettes and their accessories, regardless of quantity or personal use. Import penalty on summary conviction: a fine of HK$500,000 and two years' imprisonment.

notes: Since 30 April 2026 it is also an offence to possess a specified alternative smoking product in a public place: a HK$3,000 fixed penalty for small non-commercial quantities (up to 5 capsules / 5 mL / 100 heat sticks / 100 rolls), or a fine of up to HK$10,000 on conviction, and up to HK$50,000 and six months' imprisonment for larger quantities. Don't pack a vape, pods or heat sticks for Hong Kong, even in checked luggage; the Tobacco and Alcohol Control Office page doesn't describe any personal-use exception.

legal_source.name: Tobacco and Alcohol Control Office, Department of Health — Ban on Alternative Smoking Products

limits.description: Cannabis is a dangerous drug under the Dangerous Drugs Ordinance (Cap. 134). Hong Kong Customs "reminds members of the public not to bring any cannabis products or products containing CBD into Hong Kong." Trafficking (including importing and exporting) carries a maximum penalty of a fine of HK$5 million and life imprisonment; possession and consumption carry up to HK$1 million and seven years' imprisonment.

notes: There is no medical or personal-use exception for travellers, and no THC threshold. Edibles, oils, vape cartridges and food or drinks containing cannabis all count.

legal_source.name: Hong Kong Customs and Excise Department — Customs takes strict enforcement action to control cannabidiol (CBD) from February 1 (press release)

limits.description: "CBD has been listed as a dangerous drug under the Dangerous Drugs Ordinance (DDO)" since 1 February 2023. "Importation of products (including food or drinks) containing CBD into Hong Kong is prohibited unless the relevant provisions in the DDO are complied with," with no exemption based on concentration. Maximum penalty for trafficking (including import): HK$5 million and life imprisonment; for possession or consumption: HK$1 million and seven years.

notes: Unlike most of the world, Hong Kong treats even zero-THC CBD as a dangerous drug: skin care, edible oils and supplements containing CBD are all covered. The Narcotics Division adds that CBD products can contain trace THC and that CBD can decompose into THC in storage.

legal_source.name: Narcotics Division, Security Bureau — Legislative Control of Cannabidiol (CBD)

limits.description: "Pharmaceutical products and medicines imported in the personal baggage of a person entering Hong Kong and which are accompanied by him and in a reasonable quantity for his personal use may be exempted from licensing requirement." No numeric day-supply cap is published; "reasonable quantity for personal use" is the test.

notes: This exemption covers ordinary medicines. Medicines containing dangerous drugs (see the controlled-medication entry for Hong Kong) need prior written approval from the Drug Office. Medicines containing endangered-species ingredients need separate approval under species-protection law.

legal_source.name: Drug Office, Department of Health — Frequently Asked Questions (medicines carried by visitors)

limits.description: A visitor wishing to bring medicine containing dangerous drugs (as defined under the Dangerous Drugs Ordinance, Cap. 134) must obtain "prior written approval issued by the Drug Office of the Department of Health", supported by a certification letter from the local doctor giving the doctor's name and medical registration number, clinic details, the patient's name and address, and the drug name, dosage form, strength and total quantity, with the doctor's original signature. Processing normally takes 10 working days; carry both the letter and the approval while travelling.

notes: Customs' list of dangerous drugs includes opium, morphine, heroin, cannabis, cocaine and amphetamines, so amphetamine-based ADHD medication such as Adderall falls in this approval regime (an inference from that list). Which other prescription drugs (for example specific benzodiazepines or methylphenidate brands) are scheduled under Cap. 134 was not confirmed in this pass — ask the Drug Office (tel. +852 2572 2068, pharmgeneral@dh.gov.hk) before travelling with them.

legal_source.name: Drug Office, Department of Health — Frequently Asked Questions (medicines carried by visitors)

limits.description: "No licence is required for the import of frozen or chilled meat and poultry imported in the personal baggage of a person for personal consumption or as gifts, in an amount not exceeding 15 kg. For frozen or chilled meat and poultry, however, an official certificate as defined in the Imported Game, Meat, Poultry and Eggs Regulations, Cap. 132AK, is required."
limits.quantity: 15 kg meat/poultry, with an official certificate

notes: The licence exemption up to 15 kg comes with a requirement for an official health certificate from the exporting country, which ordinary travellers rarely have — treat homemade or shop-bought meat as something to leave behind unless you hold one. Milk and milk beverages, and eggs, are listed as having their own specific legal requirements or administrative arrangements, which this page doesn't spell out, so no dairy allowance is stated here.

legal_source.name: Hong Kong Customs and Excise Department — Controlled Imports

limits.description: "Under the Plant (Importation and Pest Control) Ordinance, Cap. 207, it is illegal to import plants, plant pests or soil into Hong Kong without a valid licence / authorization issued in advance by the Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department. However, plants produced in and imported from any place in China outside Hong Kong are exempted from licensing requirement. The exemption also applies to the import of cut flowers, fruits and vegetables for consumption."

notes: So fresh fruit and vegetables for your own consumption and cut flowers need no plant licence, but live plants, seeds-for-planting and soil do (in advance). General food-safety law still applies to food you bring. Endangered plant species and derivatives need a separate advance licence under Cap. 586.

legal_source.name: Hong Kong Customs and Excise Department — Controlled Imports

limits.description: Under the Firearms and Ammunition Ordinance, Cap. 238, "possession of arms and ammunition is subject to a licence for possession or a dealer's licence issued by the Hong Kong Police Force." "Arms" include pistols, air guns and air rifles with muzzle energy greater than 2 joules, electric stun guns, aerosols containing noxious gas, liquid or powder (e.g. dog repellents), harpoons, spear guns, and crossbows with a draw weight of more than 6 kg. Importing arms and ammunition on the Munitions List also requires a licence from the Trade and Industry Department. Separately, the Weapons Ordinance, Cap. 217, "forbids the possession of the prohibited weapons, such as Chinese-style throwing dart, knuckleduster, spring-loaded steel baton, gravity knife and gravity-operated steel baton, as listed in the Schedule of the Ordinance."

notes: The page describes a licensing system for arms, not a route for tourists to obtain a licence — treat firearms, air guns, stun guns, pepper spray and crossbows as do-not-pack. The prohibited-weapons list is a possession ban with no licence route stated; it names knuckledusters, gravity knives and spring-loaded batons. Ordinary knives that aren't on the Schedule aren't addressed by this page.

legal_source.name: Hong Kong Customs and Excise Department — Controlled Imports

limits.description: Under Hong Kong's Small Unmanned Aircraft Order (Cap. 448G), "all SUA and remote pilots shall be registered except for Standard Category A1 Operations" — that is, aircraft weighing not more than 250 g operated within the applicable operating requirements are exempt from registration. Non-residents register through the Civil Aviation Department's eSUA portal using their travel documents; registrations by non-residents "are normally valid for six months."

notes: Visitors are told to apply once they have concrete travel plans and their travel documents ready; registration labels are collected in person, through an authorised representative, or delivered by local surface mail to a Hong Kong address (no international courier). Anything over 250 g should be registered before you fly it, so plan ahead rather than sorting it out at the airport. The page excerpt read here doesn't detail the heavier categories' operating rules or insurance requirements.

legal_source.name: Civil Aviation Department (Hong Kong) — Small Unmanned Aircraft Order (Cap. 448G): tips for visitors

limits.description: From outside the EU (including the UK): 1 litre of spirits, or 2 litres of other alcoholic drinks up to 22% alcohol (e.g. port, sherry, sparkling wine, some liqueurs), plus 4 litres of still wine and 16 litres of beer. You can split the spirits/other-drinks allowance fractionally (e.g. 0.5 litres of spirits and 1 litre of port). Customs Duty, Excise Duty and VAT apply to anything above the allowance.

notes: Applies to travellers aged 17 or over (Revenue/Citizens Information: "You are not entitled to alcohol or tobacco allowances if you are under 17"). This is Ireland's own Revenue guidance for arrivals from outside the EU (including Great Britain). Reduced allowances apply to transport crews (0.35 L spirits, 0.75 L still wine, 4 L beer). Arrivals from within the EU follow different rules.

legal_source.name: Revenue (Ireland) — Duty-free allowances (travelling from outside the EU)

limits.description: From outside the EU (including the UK): 200 cigarettes, or 100 cigarillos, or 50 cigars, or 250g of smoking tobacco. The allowance can be split fractionally (e.g. 100 cigarettes and 50 cigarillos). Duty and VAT apply above it.

notes: Revenue: "The import of oral smokeless tobacco is generally prohibited" (snus-type products) — see Ireland's prohibitions and restrictions list. Reduced allowances apply to transport crews (40 cigarettes, 20 cigarillos, 10 cigars or 50g).

legal_source.name: Revenue (Ireland) — Duty-free allowances (travelling from outside the EU)

limits.description: If you enter or leave the EU at an Irish airport or port carrying cash of €10,000 or more (or the equivalent in another currency), you must make a declaration to Customs. "Cash" includes banknotes and coins, cheques/travellers' cheques/promissory notes/money orders without a named beneficiary, gold coins of at least 90% gold and gold bars/nuggets of at least 99.5% gold. The rule applies to movements to or from the UK (including the Isle of Man and Channel Islands) but not to or from Northern Ireland.

notes: A Customs officer may search for, seize and retain cash of €1,000 or more if there are reasonable grounds to believe it is proceeds of crime or intended for criminal conduct. Incorrect or incomplete declarations carry penalties.

legal_source.name: Revenue (Ireland) — Travelling with, or sending, cash

limits.description: Personal consignments of meat, milk or their products are not allowed from non-EU countries (including Great Britain), with a narrow exception for products from the Faroe Islands or Greenland (10 kg combined). Allowed in luggage from outside the EU: powdered infant milk/infant formula and special foods required for medical reasons (combined 2 kg, sealed and branded); fish and shellfish up to 20 kg or the weight of one fish; other animal products such as honey up to 2 kg; and a defined list of low-risk products (bread, cakes, biscuits, chocolate and confectionery, pasta and noodles not mixed with meat, soup stocks and flavourings, coffee/tea extracts, liqueurs and cordials).

notes: Live animals (including live insects) may not be brought in luggage from non-EU countries. The rule covers goods moving from Great Britain but not from Northern Ireland. Meat/milk personal imports can carry Foot and Mouth Disease and African Swine Fever, which is why the ban applies even to small quantities and to online orders by post or courier.

legal_source.name: Food Safety Authority of Ireland — Personal Imports (food that can be brought from a third country for personal use); Department of Agriculture, Food and the Marine — Personal Consignments in Luggage

limits.description: Plants, fruit, vegetables, cut flowers, seeds, soil and timber may not be brought in from a third country (including Great Britain) without a phytosanitary certificate presented to the Department of Agriculture, Food and the Marine at the point of entry. Bananas, durians, dates, pineapples and coconuts are exempt from phytosanitary certification. Separately, for food safety, foods of non-animal origin on the EU high-risk import-control list (Regulation (EU) 2019/1793) are limited to 5 kg of each fresh product and 2 kg of each other product in personal luggage; foods not on that list have no weight limit.

notes: The plant-health rule (certificate) and the food-safety rule (weight limits) are separate — a phytosanitary certificate is what a traveller would need for fresh produce and plants, which in practice means most fresh fruit, vegetables and plants should not be brought from outside the EU. Applies to Great Britain but not Northern Ireland.

legal_source.name: Department of Agriculture, Food and the Marine — Information on Personal Consignments in Luggage or through Postal, Courier & Online Services

notes: Citizens Information: "It is an offence to import or carry on your person, controlled substances (drugs) when travelling to or from Ireland. Examples of controlled substances are cannabis, cocaine, heroin, and amphetamines." Customs runs a National Drugs Team with detector-dog units at airports and ferry ports. Revenue lists "illegal or dangerous drugs" among goods that must be declared to a customs officer. Medicines containing controlled drugs are handled separately (see the controlled-medication entry).

legal_source.name: Citizens Information — Customs regulations for travellers to Ireland (drugs)

limits.description: Visitors from non-Schengen countries may bring up to 3 months' supply of prescription medicines for their own personal use. The Department of Health recommends original packaging with your name clearly displayed, plus the prescription (or a copy) and/or a letter from your doctor or dispensing pharmacist outlining your condition and stating the medicines are for personal use — placed inside the package as proof of legitimacy.

notes: "In Ireland, the current practice is that the customs officer must be satisfied that the documentation supports the amount and personal use of the medical products in the possession of the traveller" and "the Irish Customs Authority has the final say in all such matters." Revenue lists medicines among goods that must be declared. Medicines containing controlled drugs are covered separately (see the controlled-medication entry).

legal_source.name: Department of Health (Ireland) — Travelling into Ireland with prescribed narcotics and/or psychotropic substances

limits.description: From non-Schengen countries (e.g. US, UK, Canada, Australia, Asia): the Department of Health's general rule applies — up to 3 months' supply for personal use, original packaging, and a prescription or doctor's/pharmacist's letter inside the package; a customs officer must be satisfied the documents support the amount and personal use. From Schengen countries (since 1 April 2023): an Article 75 Certificate issued or authenticated by your own country's competent authority is required for any prescribed product containing a controlled drug in Schedule II or III of the Misuse of Drugs Regulations 2017, with a separate certificate for each drug. Prescribed cannabis-based products are not permitted to be brought into Ireland.

notes: Ireland's own statute (Misuse of Drugs Regulations 2017, S.I. 173/2017) lists amphetamine, dexamphetamine, lisdexamfetamine, methylphenidate (Ritalin/Concerta), oxycodone, methadone, buprenorphine and fentanyl in Schedule 2, so ADHD stimulants and strong opioids are Schedule 2 drugs — and need the Article 75 Certificate when arriving from a Schengen country. Alprazolam (Xanax), diazepam (Valium) and zolpidem are in Schedule 4, which the Department's Article 75 rule does not cover. Methadone and buprenorphine for opioid substitution may be brought in from the Schengen Area with an Article 75 Certificate. To check a specific product's schedule, use the HPRA 'search for a medicine' tool; for personal-medication queries the Department points to enforcementcontrol@hpra.ie. The Department page describes the non-Schengen rule in general terms only and does not name a separate certificate for non-Schengen visitors — carry full documentation regardless, since Irish Customs has the final say.

legal_source.name: Department of Health (Ireland) — Travelling into Ireland with prescribed narcotics and/or psychotropic substances

limits.description: Flying a drone in Ireland that weighs more than 250 grams, or has a camera or sensor, requires registration as a drone operator with the Irish Aviation Authority (IAA). Registration costs €41 and is valid for 2 years; you then label the drone with your operator registration number and load it into the drone's Direct Remote ID. Drones over 250g also need online-training certification (valid 5 years). Open-category flights are for drones under 25 kg (or with a class mark 0–4); heavier drones cannot be flown without IAA permission. If you live in the EU you only register in your country of residence, not in each country you fly in.

notes: This is a flight-operation rule, not a customs ban — bringing a drone into Ireland isn't itself restricted, but flying it legally is. The IAA or the Gardaí can take away a drone if they believe it is likely to be used in breach of the regulations, and flying a drone with a camera over identifiable people can raise privacy offences. The Citizens Information and IAA pages do not spell out a separate route for non-EU visitors who aren't registered in an EU state — confirm the process with the IAA (MySRS) before travelling rather than assuming registration can be done on arrival.

legal_source.name: Citizens Information — Owning and operating a drone (summarising Irish Aviation Authority rules; IAA registration page: https://www.iaa.ie/general-aviation/drones/drone-register)

limits.description: Firearms need an importation (transfer) licence from the Department of Justice obtained BEFORE bringing them into the country, plus firearms certification; a firearms certificate for a non-resident costs €40 for 1 year. CS gas spray, pepper spray and stun guns are totally prohibited: importation or possession is illegal. Crossbows, spearguns and all airguns with a muzzle velocity over 1 joule (including paintball markers) are legally firearms and must be licensed. The Firearms and Offensive Weapons Act 1990 prohibits importing offensive weapons (listed in the 1991 Order, as amended in 2009 — including flick knives and several disguised knives), with penalties of up to 10 years' imprisonment.

notes: Other types of knives can be imported, but carrying one in public without lawful reason is an offence under Section 9 of the 1990 Act, so a knife in luggage is not the same as a knife on your person. Antique firearms held as ornaments or curiosities are exempt from the Firearms Acts, but the licensing position for an ordinary traveller is: don't bring a firearm without written authorisation. Revenue also lists "firearms, weapons, fireworks or explosives" among goods that must be declared to a customs officer.

legal_source.name: Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration — Firearms: your questions answered

limits.description: The Food Safety Authority of Ireland states CBD "is not considered a narcotic drug and is not a controlled drug in Ireland under the Misuse of Drugs Act 1977" — but THC is: "There is no legal threshold or tolerance in Ireland under the Misuse of Drugs Act for the presence of THC in food, except for hemp seed and hemp seed derived food products", so food products containing THC at any level (other than hemp seed products) are classified as controlled drugs. Separately, CBD as or in food or food supplements is an unauthorised novel food under EU Regulation 2015/2283 and cannot legally be placed on the EU market.

notes: The FSAI page is about placing products on the market and about what counts as a controlled drug; it does not give a traveller-specific rule for CBD in personal luggage. Practical reading: a CBD product with any measurable THC is a controlled-drug risk at the border; a genuinely THC-free product isn't a controlled drug, but can't be lawfully sold as a food supplement. Hemp seeds and hemp seed oil/flour are outside both the Misuse of Drugs Act and the novel food rules. Prescribed cannabis-based medicines are not permitted to be brought into Ireland (Department of Health).

legal_source.name: Food Safety Authority of Ireland — Regulation of Cannabidiol (CBD) and Hemp food products in Ireland

limits.description: Revenue's traveller allowances for arrivals from outside the EU list allowances for cigarettes, cigarillos, cigars and smoking tobacco only — there is no vaping-specific allowance, and Revenue's list of prohibited/restricted goods in baggage does not mention e-cigarettes or vapes. Since 1 November 2025 Ireland charges an E-Liquid Products Tax of 50 cent per millilitre on e-liquid (nicotine and non-nicotine), but Revenue says it applies "the first time an e-liquid product is supplied by a business in the State", i.e. it falls on importers, manufacturers and suppliers, not on a traveller's own device.

notes: This row records what the traveller guidance does and doesn't say — no source found either sets a personal-import quantity for vapes or bans carrying one. Whether e-liquid in luggage is treated under the general €430 goods allowance is not stated by Revenue and is an inference, not a confirmed rule. Vapes are regulated at the point of sale (nicotine inhaling products licence, no sale to under-18s, under the Public Health (Tobacco Products and Nicotine Inhaling Products) Act 2023), which is a retail rule rather than a border one.

legal_source.name: Revenue (Ireland) — Revenue publishes guidance on new 'Vape Tax' (E-Liquid Products Tax); traveller allowances page: https://www.revenue.ie/en/customs/individuals/info-travelling-duty-free/from-outside-eu/allowances.aspx

limits.description: Wine, spirits, beer or malt liquor: not exceeding 1 litre in total is exempt from customs duty/tax, for travellers entering by air or any other mode of transport. Anything above that is dutiable and must be declared in the Red Lane.

notes: Per the Customs Department's Traveler's Guide list of goods exempt from duty/tax. The page does not state the rules on alcohol for Muslim travellers or any minimum-age rule, and those were not checked.

legal_source.name: Royal Malaysian Customs Department — Traveler's Guide

limits.description: Cigarettes and tobacco products are not on the Customs Department's list of duty-free goods for travellers — they are expressly excluded from the general exemption — so any quantity is dutiable and must be declared in the Red Lane.

notes: The Traveler's Guide gives no duty-free tobacco quantity and only says duty/tax on tobacco follows a 'specific' rate under the Sales Tax (Rate of Tax) Order 2018; the per-stick rate was not confirmed. Some secondary sources describe an older 200-cigarette allowance — the current official page does not list one.

legal_source.name: Royal Malaysian Customs Department — Traveler's Guide

limits.description: Cash and bearer negotiable instruments amounting to USD 10,000 or more (entering or leaving) must be declared on Customs Form No. 7 at the customs counters. Importing or exporting Malaysian ringgit requires prior written permission from Bank Negara Malaysia.

notes: Legal basis: s.28B(1) Anti-Money Laundering, Anti-Terrorism Financing and Proceeds of Unlawful Activities Act 2001 and Regulation 55, Customs Regulations 2019. Failure to declare is an offence punishable by a fine of up to RM3 million or up to 5 years' imprisonment, or both.

legal_source.name: Royal Malaysian Customs Department — Traveler's Guide

notes: Import and export of drugs including morphine, heroin, opium and cannabis is strictly prohibited. Under the Customs Act 1967 and the Dangerous Drugs Act 1952 the penalty for drug trafficking is a mandatory death penalty. There is no recreational or medical-cannabis exception for travellers on this page; prescription drugs may only be imported under Ministry of Health licences/permits.

legal_source.name: Royal Malaysian Customs Department — Traveler's Guide

limits.description: Medicines (including vitamins and supplements) for your own use or an immediate family member travelling with you: not more than the quantity reasonably needed for one (1) month's use by one person, judged from the dosage on the label. Keep the dispensing label and original packaging intact.

notes: Only products registered with the Drug Control Authority may be imported commercially; the personal-use allowance is a separate traveller exception under the Poisons Act 1952, Dangerous Drugs Act 1952 and Control of Drugs and Cosmetics Regulations 1984. If you will be in Malaysia over a month you are told to get prescriptions from a registered Malaysian doctor. Do not bring medicines for anyone other than yourself or an immediate family member travelling with you.

legal_source.name: Ministry of Health Malaysia, Pharmaceutical Services Programme — Traveller's Guide: Bringing Medication into Malaysia

limits.description: Prescription medicines containing dangerous drugs (e.g. cannabis- or narcotic-based medication liable to abuse or dependence) must be declared at the border on arrival. Medicines controlled under the Dangerous Drugs Act 1952 and the Poisons (Psychotropic Substances) Regulations 1989 need a valid prescription or a doctor's letter, written in English or with a translation, stating the medicine, dosage and quantity. The same one-month personal-use quantity cap applies.

notes: The MOH guide points to the First Schedule of the Dangerous Drugs Act 1952 and the Third Schedule of the Poisons Act 1952 for which substances are covered — this pass did not check each named drug (e.g. specific ADHD stimulants or benzodiazepines) against those schedules, so confirm a specific product with the MOH Pharmaceutical Services Programme (pelesenanbpf@moh.gov.my, +603-7841 3200/3320) before travel. The Customs Department separately states prescription drugs can only be imported subject to licences/permits from the Ministry of Health, and drug trafficking carries a mandatory death penalty.

legal_source.name: Ministry of Health Malaysia, Pharmaceutical Services Programme — Traveller's Guide: Bringing Medication into Malaysia

limits.description: Import of nicotine and of nicotine-containing preparations 'of a kind used for vaporizer smoking' (vape liquid/gel) is a conditional prohibition: it is prohibited except under an import licence from the Ministry of Health's Pharmaceutical Services Programme (Customs (Prohibition of Imports) Order 2023, Second Schedule Part I, item 4). Separately, the Customs Department's traveller duty-free list expressly excludes electronic cigarettes and vaporising devices and their liquids, so they are dutiable and must be declared in the Red Lane.

notes: Neither the Order nor the Traveler's Guide sets a personal-use quantity or grants travellers an exemption from the licence requirement — treat carrying nicotine vape liquid as risky and check with Malaysian Customs or the Ministry of Health first. Vaping products are also regulated under the Control of Smoking Products for Public Health Act 2024 (Act 852, in force 1 October 2024); that Act's own text and any traveller-specific provisions were not read in this pass.

legal_source.name: Customs (Prohibition of Imports) Order 2023, P.U.(A) 117 — Malaysia Attorney General's Chambers

limits.description: Import is allowed only with a licence or approval from the Chief Police Officer: arms and ammunition as defined in the Arms Act 1960 (including paintball markers/pellets and Taser guns), shotgun cartridges, expandable batons, imitation arms including toy guns and pistols, and imitation hand grenades (Arms Act 1960); fireworks and explosives (Explosives Act 1957). A traveller without that licence cannot lawfully bring them in.

notes: From the Customs (Prohibition of Imports) Order 2023, Third Schedule items 44–50. Ordinary pocket knives and multitools are not addressed by these items and were not researched separately.

legal_source.name: Customs (Prohibition of Imports) Order 2023, P.U.(A) 117 — Malaysia Attorney General's Chambers

limits.description: Import of meat and edible meat offal, dairy produce, birds' eggs and honey, and of any domestic animal or its meat/eggs, requires prior official approval: a MAQIS import permit and inspection (Malaysian Quarantine and Inspection Services Act 2011) and, for food products, approval of the Ministry of Health's Food Safety and Quality Division (Customs (Prohibition of Imports) Order 2023).

notes: No traveller exemption or personal-quantity allowance appears in the Order. Enforcement is real: Malaysia's state news reported MAQIS seizing 40 pork sausages and 10 chickens from a passenger at KLIA in 2025 for lacking a MAQIS import permit and an origin-country health certificate, under s.11(1) of Act 728. The Customs Traveler's Guide separately lists 'food preparations' up to RM150 as duty-exempt, which is a duty rule and does not override the permit requirement.

legal_source.name: Customs (Prohibition of Imports) Order 2023, P.U.(A) 117 — Malaysia Attorney General's Chambers

limits.description: Edible vegetables and roots, fruit and nuts, coffee/tea/spices and cereals are food products whose import is subject to the approval of the Ministry of Health's Food Safety and Quality Division (Customs (Prohibition of Imports) Order 2023, Third Schedule item 35). Importing plants, agricultural produce or soil without a valid MAQIS import permit is an offence under the MAQIS Act 2011.

notes: No personal-luggage exemption or quantity allowance appears in the Order or on the MAQIS FAQ. Live plants, seeds and cut flowers were not separately confirmed on a primary page in this pass.

legal_source.name: Customs (Prohibition of Imports) Order 2023, P.U.(A) 117 — Malaysia Attorney General's Chambers

limits.description: Under regulation 140 of the Civil Aviation Regulations 2016, anyone intending to operate an Unmanned Aircraft System must obtain prior authorisation from CAAM. For low-risk operations (visual line of sight, under 400 ft above ground, no spraying) that authorisation is an Authorisation to Fly (ATF) permit, applied for by email to drone.atf@caam.gov.my at least 14 working days before the flight; flying without the required permit is a violation penalised under regulation 206(3).

notes: This is a flight-operation requirement, not a customs import ban. CAAM's notice says nothing about a tourist or recreational exemption, so plan on an ATF permit for any flight. Widely reported figures — a RM250 permit fee, registration of drones above 250 g, a RM50,000 maximum fine — appear only in secondary sources and were not confirmed on a CAAM page in this pass; whether importing a consumer drone needs a separate approval (e.g. radio-equipment certification) was also not confirmed.

legal_source.name: Civil Aviation Authority of Malaysia (CAAM) — Safety Information 01/2025: Authorisation to Fly (ATF) application for UAS operations

limits.description: Duty-free for passengers aged 18 or over, in hand luggage/baggage for personal or family use or as a gift, per 30 calendar days: 1 litre of spirits of 22% ABV or higher (or undenatured ethyl alcohol of 80% or higher), OR 2 litres of alcoholic beverages under 22% ABV, OR a combination of those two kinds within their percentage shares (beer and wine excepted from the combination); PLUS 4 litres of wine AND 16 litres of beer.
limits.quantity: 1 L spirits (22%+) or 2 L under 22%; plus 4 L wine and 16 L beer

notes: Quoted from the Revenue Service's own brochure. It states the allowances "per 30 calendar days" for goods entering through land and marine checkpoints; the air-checkpoint paragraph prints "per calendar days" (the "30" appears to have been dropped), and the brochure states the same volumes for air, so treat 30 days as the intended period but confirm at the airport if you're near the limit. Anything above the allowance is dutiable and must be declared.

legal_source.name: Revenue Service of Georgia — Exemption from import duties and the obligation of declaring goods carried by an individual (customs brochure)

limits.description: Duty-free for passengers aged 18 or over, in hand luggage/baggage for personal or family use or as a gift, per 30 calendar days on land/sea entries (the air paragraph gives the same quantities): 200 cigarettes, OR 50 cigars, OR 50 cigarillos, OR 200 heated-tobacco sticks, OR 10 tobacco capsules, OR 250 g of other tobacco (raw tobacco excluded), or a combination as long as the percentage shares of each product's limit total no more than 100%.
limits.quantity: 200 cigarettes, or 50 cigars, or 50 cigarillos, or 200 heated-tobacco sticks, or 250 g other tobacco

notes: Quoted from the Revenue Service's own brochure. Electronic-cigarette liquid has its own separate 50 ml allowance inside the same tobacco allowance — see the e-cigarettes entry for Georgia.

legal_source.name: Revenue Service of Georgia — Exemption from import duties and the obligation of declaring goods carried by an individual (customs brochure)

limits.description: Within the same passenger tobacco allowance (aged 18+, hand luggage/baggage, personal or family use or as a gift), the Revenue Service's brochure allows 50 ml of electronic-cigarette liquid duty-free per 30 calendar days. E-cigarette liquid is expressly excluded from the general GEL 500 / GEL 3,000 goods-value allowance and from the food allowance, so it can't be brought in under those.

notes: This covers the customs duty-free allowance for e-liquid only. The brochure doesn't address vaping devices themselves, nicotine strength limits, or Georgia's domestic tobacco-control rules for e-cigarettes, and no separate Georgian import ban on devices was found in this pass — confirm devices and pods with Georgian Customs if you're carrying more than a personal setup.

legal_source.name: Revenue Service of Georgia — Exemption from import duties and the obligation of declaring goods carried by an individual (customs brochure)

limits.description: An individual must declare cash (national and/or foreign currency), cheques and/or securities with a total sum of more than GEL 30,000 (or the equivalent in another currency) when importing or exporting them.

notes: The threshold applies to both bringing money in and taking it out, and covers cheques and securities as well as banknotes. Quoted from the Revenue Service's brochure ('When is an individual obliged to declare goods?'). Penalties for failing to declare aren't stated in the brochure, so none are asserted here.

legal_source.name: Revenue Service of Georgia — Exemption from import duties and the obligation of declaring goods carried by an individual (customs brochure)

limits.description: "A person can bring into the territory of Georgia 31 days’ supply of narcotic drugs and psychotropic substances for personal use (except of “narcotic drugs strictly restricted for free circulation” included in the list 1 of annex 1 of law of Georgia on “Narcotic drugs, psychotropic substances, Precursors and Narcological Assistance”)." You must present, together with your customs declaration: a photocopy of the prescription translated into English and certified by an apostille (name, surname, gender and age, diagnosis, brand and generic names, dosage form, quantity, method of use and duration of treatment); the prescribing physician’s certificate, translated into English and certified per the law of the departure country; and a document signed and sealed by an authorised person and apostilled (authority name, address, contact person, phone, country of destination).

notes: Customs checks the documents against what you carry, signs and seals them and returns them to you; keep them for your whole stay (handing them in on departure is not mandatory). Anything on List 1 of Annex 1 cannot be brought in even with a prescription. Which specific brand-name drugs (e.g. amphetamine-based stimulants) sit on List 1 versus the permitted lists was not confirmed in this pass — the Ministry of Foreign Affairs publishes the schedules separately, so check your exact medicine against them before travel. The Revenue Service’s brochure also lists narcotic drugs, psychotropic substances and "medications subject to the special control" among goods needing permits/certificates.

legal_source.name: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Georgia — Bringing Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances to Georgia (official guidance PDF)

notes: Georgia's Constitutional Court ruled on 30 July 2018 that consuming cannabis is protected private conduct, and a follow-up law limits consumption to adults 21+ at home — but that did not legalise acquiring, carrying or importing it, and the substances above remain on the strictly-restricted list. Press reporting on the follow-up law (OC Media) describes continuing penalties for possession and acquisition: fines from GEL 500 for a first offence, criminal fines of at least GEL 1,500 or community work for repeats within a year, GEL 800–1,500 for public consumption, and 6–10 years' imprisonment for supplying under-21s. Do not bring cannabis into Georgia.

legal_source.name: Law of Georgia on Narcotic Drugs, Psychotropic Substances, Precursors and Narcological Assistance — Annex 1 List I and Art. 30(4) (matsne.gov.ge)

limits.description: Cannabis (flowering or fruiting tops), cannabis extracts and tinctures, cannabis oil and cannabis resin are all listed in Annex 1, List I of Georgia's narcotics law — the list of "narcotic drugs strictly restricted for free circulation." The Ministry of Foreign Affairs' traveller guidance excludes List 1 substances from the 31-day personal-supply allowance that applies to prescribed narcotic medicines, and under Art. 30(4) narcotic drugs brought in without a preliminary permit are returned at the supplier's expense.

The Revenue Service brochure lists "Plant and / or animal, their parts or derivatives" among the goods for which permits and/or certificates must be submitted additionally at customs (it applies to any import that is restricted or requires a permit or license, which must be declared).

notes: The brochure gives no personal-luggage quantity or exemption and doesn’t say which meat or dairy products are covered, so this row only establishes that animal products need permits/certificates in principle. The National Food Agency issues the veterinary-control import permits (reported as valid for one month, applied for electronically); its traveller-specific guidance and the Revenue Service’s "Plants and Animals" FAQ page are not readable without a browser, so confirm with the National Food Agency before bringing meat or dairy.

legal_source.name: Revenue Service of Georgia — customs brochure "Exemption of goods from duties and declaring" (section: goods requiring permits and/or certificates)

limits.description: The Revenue Service brochure lists "Plant and / or animal, their parts or derivatives" among the goods for which permits and/or certificates must be submitted additionally at customs (any import that is restricted or requires a permit or license must be declared).

Phytosanitary import permits are issued by the National Food Agency (reported validity up to 6 months); its traveller guidance and the Revenue Service’s "Plants and Animals" FAQ page could not be read, so check with the National Food Agency before bringing fruit, vegetables, seeds or plants.

legal_source.name: Revenue Service of Georgia — customs brochure "Exemption of goods from duties and declaring" (section: goods requiring permits and/or certificates)

notes: In practice this means firearms, ammunition and explosives cannot simply be carried in; a permit from the competent Georgian authority is required first. The brochure doesn’t say which authority issues permits for visitors, or how knives, air weapons and self-defence sprays are treated — don’t assume an ordinary tourist can obtain a permit, and check with Georgian authorities before travelling with anything that could be classed as a weapon.

limits.description: Georgia’s Civil Aviation Agency drone portal uses the EU-style class system (class C0: MTOM under 250 g; C2: under 4 kg; C3/C4: under 25 kg), asks users to "label your unmanned aircraft with your user registration number before heading out to fly", limits several classes to "a maximum attainable height above the take-off point limited to 120 m", and states that "Flying UAS within Restricted, Prohibited and Dangerous areas without authorization is not permitted" (zone information at airspace.gov.ge).

notes: The official portal page does not say who must register, or whether a foreign visitor can register or fly a drone brought from abroad; secondary sources say drones over 250 g need GCAA registration but that is unconfirmed here. Customs also treats high-frequency radio-electronic devices and communication equipment as permit goods (Revenue Service brochure) — whether that reaches consumer drones is not stated. Register or check with the Civil Aviation Agency before flying.

legal_source.name: Maldives Airports Company — Velana International Airport: Customs & Security, Prohibited & Restricted Items

legal_source.name: Maldives Airports Company — Velana International Airport: Customs & Security, Prohibited & Restricted Items

legal_source.name: Maldives Airports Company — Velana International Airport: Customs & Security, Prohibited & Restricted Items

legal_source.name: Maldives Airports Company — Velana International Airport: Customs & Security, Prohibited & Restricted Items

limits.description: MFDA Guideline on Good Import Practice §4.7: "Importation of medicines for personal use will be limited to 90 days' supply"; more than 90 days needs additional documents on the patient's illness history (up to 6 months' supply with them). notes: The airport operator's customs page: prescription medication "may be imported for personal use with a valid prescription or doctor's letter issued by a registered medical practitioner", in original pharmacy packaging with clear labelling and "not in excessive amounts relative to your time in the Maldives"; carrying it without valid documentation may lead to confiscation or investigation. The 90-day figure and prescription details come from the MFDA import guideline, which is written for importers as well as individuals — check with MFDA for anything beyond a routine supply.

legal_source.name: Maldives Food and Drug Authority — Guideline on Good Import Practice (MTG/RE-IP/GLN-TE 007, 13.02.2020), §§4.7–4.9

limits.description: MFDA Guideline §4.9.1: "Importation of controlled drug for prescription should be limited to 30 days' supply, for patients with chronic illness can be of maximum 90 days' supply"; more than three months needs documents on the patient's illness history with a valid prescription, and a controlled-drug prescription is valid for 90 days from the prescribed date. §4.8.2: "It is an offense to import any controlled drug into Maldives without obtaining the import certificate from MFDA", and controlled medicinal products may not be imported by post.

The MFDA guideline requires an MFDA import certificate/authorization for controlled drugs and channels bulk imports through designated importers; how that applies to a traveller's personal supply is not spelled out, so contact MFDA before travelling with any narcotic or psychotropic medicine (that includes ADHD stimulants and benzodiazepines). legal_source.name: Maldives Food and Drug Authority — Guideline on Good Import Practice (MTG/RE-IP/GLN-TE 007, 13.02.2020), §§4.7–4.9

limits.description: Effective 9 November 2024, only travellers on a tourist visa may import limited tobacco for personal use, duty-exempt: "Up to 200 cigarettes, or 25 cigars, or 250 grams of tobacco." legal_source.name: Maldives Customs Service — Circular 14-VDS/CIR/2024/2 (9 Nov 2024): Revised Guidelines on Importation of Tobacco Products by Travellers

The airport operator's customs page adds: "Permits required in advance from MCAA + MNDF. Drones without permits may be held at customs", and lists drones without permits among items given a retrieval receipt at the border.

legal_source.name: Maldives Civil Aviation Authority — Flying Remotely Piloted Aircraft (Drones) in the Maldives

legal_source.name: Maldives Airports Company — Velana International Airport: Customs & Security, Prohibited & Restricted Items

legal_source.name: Maldives Airports Company — Velana International Airport: Customs & Security, Prohibited & Restricted Items

limits.description: Quoted directly from Customs: "1 liter of spirits or 1 liter of sparkling and liqueur wines or suitable combination of mentioned drinks and 1 liter of other wines" may be brought duty-free as personal luggage. legal_source.name: Customs Administration of the Republic of Serbia — Passenger Customs Clearance FAQ (Tourists)

limits.description: Quoted directly from Customs: "50 cigarettes, 25 cigarillos (cigars up to 3g), 10 cigars, 50g of tobacco or suitable combination of all mentioned products." This covers cut tobacco, pipe tobacco, hookah tobacco, chewing tobacco, snuff, and heated (non-burning) tobacco products. Oral tobacco (snus) is explicitly excluded: "tobacco for oral use (snus) whose import and distribution in the Republic of Serbia is prohibited."

notes: Marked "depends" because the allowance covers most tobacco forms but snus specifically is prohibited outright, not just capped. Above the allowance, duty/VAT applies (10% flat rate under EUR 3,000 total dutiable value; regular procedure above that).

legal_source.name: Customs Administration of the Republic of Serbia — Passenger Customs Clearance FAQ (Tourists)
